title: How to work stem stitch in cross-stitch
subtitle: A twisted line stitch for outlines and botanical stems
excerpt: Stem stitch is a line stitch worked by overlapping small forward stitches with the thread held to one side, producing a smooth twisted rope along the line. In cross-stitch pieces it appears in the back-stitch layer as an alternative to straight back-stitch when a more textured outline suits the design.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776, outline stitch section. William Morris-period embroidery treatises, public domain.

glossaryTerms.definition: A line stitch where small forward stitches overlap with the thread held consistently to one side, producing a smooth twisted rope along the stitched line.

A solid outline stitch worked in a single strand along the back-stitch layer of the chart. You stitch backwards along the line one stitch at a time, each stitch finishing where the previous one started.

A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads. The default for beginners. Counted in squares per inch: 11ct, 14ct, 16ct, and 18ct are the common counts.

The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch. Each skein is made of six strands twisted together loosely; the stitcher strips out the number of strands needed for the fabric count (two strands for 14-count Aida) and threads them together.

content.text: is a forward line stitch where each new stitch starts slightly behind the finish point of the previous one, with the thread held to the same side each time. The result is a tight twisted rope that curves smoothly and looks fuller than a simple
In cross-stitch pieces, stem stitch is most at home on botanical subjects where a back-stitch outline reads too flat for a thick stem or a curved branch. Work it in a single strand on 14-count
for a fine rope; two strands give a heavier, more visible line. The stitches run diagonally across the fabric threads, so the line does not follow the grid holes as strictly as back-stitch does.
Come up at the start of the line. Decide whether to hold the
above or below the needle throughout. Pick one side and keep it for the entire line or the twist will lose its consistency.
Insert the needle a short distance along the line (roughly two to three Aida squares for 14-count) and bring it back up halfway between the start and the insertion point.
The floss should be on the chosen side as the needle exits. Pull through gently without snagging the thread that is already sitting on the surface.
Continue along the line. Each new stitch starts exactly where the previous one ended, maintaining the overlap. The twisted rope builds as the stitches accumulate.
At the end of the line, take the needle down to the back at the last exit point and finish with the standard thread-ending method.

items.symptom: The twist disappears or reverses partway along the line
items.cause: The thread was held on alternating sides as each stitch was formed.
items.fix: Hold the thread to the same side, consistently, for every stitch on the same line. If the twist vanishes, restart the section.

items.symptom: The stitch looks more like back-stitch than a rope
items.cause: Each stitch is starting too far back from the previous exit point.
items.fix: The overlap should be roughly half a stitch length. Bring the needle up closer to the previous insertion point to tighten the rope.

content.text: Stem stitch is best applied in project tutorials with botanical subjects. Try it on a florals piece in place of the standard back-stitch outlines to see how much more presence the stems gain.
